tier_reason: Third-party shootout MuggleWei/cc_log_benchmark: public harness (gbenchmark/log_gbenchmark.h, gbenchmark/cpp/loguru/gbenchmark_loguru.cpp, gbenchmark/cpp/glog/gbenchmark_glog.cpp), flags from public build.sh/CMakeLists.txt (CMake Release, -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra, pinned loguru v2.1.0, glog v0.6.0, Google Benchmark v1.8.3), compiler GCC 14.2.1 and CPU i7-10710U pinned at 3.2 GHz stated in the README. Both result files (benchmark_loguru.txt, benchmark_glog.txt) are in the same report directory.

corrections.workload: Google Benchmark, one synchronous formatted INFO log call per iteration written to a log file with stderr output disabled: a message struct of four integers (u64, i64, u32, i32) and a 128-byte char string, cycling through pre-generated random messages. loguru uses printf-style LOG_F with its default unbuffered mode (g_flush_interval_ms = 0, flush per line); glog uses stream LOG(INFO) << with a custom prefix function and FLAGS_logbufsecs=0. Two scenarios: iterations:2000 x 5 repetitions at 1, 3, 6, 12 and 24 threads, and min_time 3 s at 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads. loguru v2.1.0 vs glog v0.6.0; report run 2025-02-21.
corrections.claimed_speedup: All ratios derived from page data (Time column, loguru vs glog). Iterations scenario (mean of 5): 1 thread 2392 vs 4324 ns (1.81x faster); 3 threads 4383 vs 3734 ns (glog 1.17x faster); 6 threads 4134 vs 5022 ns (1.21x); 12 threads 5398 vs 5927 ns (1.10x); 24 threads 4264 vs 5932 ns (1.39x). min_time 3 s scenario: 1 thread 2357 vs 4378 ns (1.86x); 2 threads 3265 vs 3674 ns (1.13x); 4 threads 4029 vs 4196 ns (1.04x); 8 threads 3434 vs 5357 ns (1.56x). CPU-time column favours loguru at every thread count (e.g. 24 threads 8284 vs 19366 ns). The project's own README claims 25%-75% faster than GLOG on a MacBook Pro (Clang), about the same on a Linux desktop (GCC) in unbuffered mode, and about twice as fast with ~100 ms buffered flushing.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 14.2.1 20240910, glibc 2.40; build.sh passes -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON (CMake's Release default for GCC is -O3 -DNDEBUG; not echoed in the report); CMakeLists.txt adds -Wall -Wextra and C++17; Google Benchmark v1.8.3
corrections.caveats: Benchmark is a third-party logger shootout (MuggleWei/cc_log_benchmark, 34 stars), not the loguru author's. The baseline glog v0.6.0 is old and google/glog itself was archived on 2025-06-30 (README points to ng-log and Abseil logging); loguru is v2.1.0 while the repo's latest commit bumps the version to 2.2.0. Per-line work is not identical: glog formats with iostreams and a custom prefix function and is built as a shared library (BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON), while the loguru benchmark #includes loguru.cpp into the same translation unit and prints its default prefix with uptime and thread name. The Time column for multithreaded runs is (sum of per-thread time / threads) / total calls, not single-call latency; glog wins at 3 threads (4383 vs 3734 ns) and the 4-thread min_time margin is only 1.04x. Single laptop, one run per configuration; stddev only for the iterations rows. The shootout's own conclusions single out fmtlog, haclog, Nanolog and quill as the faster libraries, not loguru. The project's own bench dirs (loguru_bench, glog_bench) are public but its README numbers give no CPU model, compiler version or glog version. Unlicense: public-domain dedication, no patent grant.

notes: All numbers match benchmark_loguru.txt and benchmark_glog.txt line for line; I rewrote claimed_speedup to list every thread count, since the old text put the 4-thread loguru win (1.04x) under 'not uniformly faster'. Metadata checks out (Unlicense, 1.9k stars, last commit 2026-09-10 'Bump version to 2.2.0', active). Shortcomings to record: not faster at 3 threads, small margins at 4 and 12 threads, baseline glog archived and pinned to v0.6.0, unequal formatting paths (iostream glog in a shared library vs printf loguru compiled inline).

tier_reason: Independent measurement: lexy's benchmark (benchmarks/json/pegtl.cpp, nlohmann.cpp, main.cpp, CMakeLists.txt) is run by the author of a competing library, not by PEGTL, with public code and the CPU stated (Apple M1 Mac Mini), but no compiler, flags or build type on the page, so it cannot reach A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the page; harness nanobench v4.3.0 (fetched in lexy benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt); compiler, flags and CMake build type unstated
corrections.caveats: The benchmark is written and run by the author of lexy, a competing parser library (already catalogued in wave 3), and PEGTL is a comparison column, not the subject; no one claims PEGTL beats nlohmann/json, the ratios are derived from the page's embedded plot data. Off-baseline for its category: the spec's parser-generators-and-combinators baselines are Bison/Flex, ANTLR, Boost.Spirit and nom, and none of them is measured; nlohmann::json::accept is a JSON library's acceptor, not its fast path, and on the same page PEGTL is slower than rapidjson SAX (2.51, 1.44, 0.97 ms), lexy (2.29, 1.08, 0.75 ms) and glaze (1.16, 0.73, 0.32 ms) on all three files. Compiler, flags and build type are not stated, and the benchmark CMake fetches PEGTL main.zip and nlohmann/json develop.zip, so versions are unpinned (page last regenerated 2025-10-13, 'Update benchmarks to include glaze'). Single Apple M1 machine, 11 samples per series. PEGTL docs mention only an internal 5-10% gain of one rule at -O0 (Rules-and-Grammars.md), not a comparison against another library. A 2018 IPSJ study compared PEGTL with Boost.Spirit.X3, cpp-peglib and matcha2 (abstract via search snippet only; per-library numbers not seen). The original category guess 'filesystems-and-io' with stdio/fstream baselines does not fit: PEGTL's file inputs (mmap_input, read_input) have no published comparison against stdio or std::fstream.

notes: Means recomputed from the 11 embedded samples match the record (canada 3.649 vs 20.199 ms, citm 2.367 vs 6.598 ms, twitter 1.406 vs 2.420 ms); pegtl.cpp runs json::text plus eof over memory_input and nlohmann.cpp calls json::accept on the same buffer. Metadata checks out (BSL-1.0, 2.2k stars, last commit 2026-10-03, active). Shortcomings to record: off-baseline (no Bison/ANTLR/Spirit/nom comparison), slower than rapidjson, lexy and glaze on the same page, compiler and flags unstated, unpinned versions.

tier_reason: The only number is a second-hand 5-10% speedup of Boost.Wave after dropping in flex_string for std::string, reported to the author and quoted in doc/flex/flex_string.html with no methodology, input, compiler or hardware; the page itself says no performance comparison suite is available.

corrections.license: MIT for the Loki library (SourceForge listing; headers such as SmallObj.h carry the MIT text); the flex_string headers carry Andrei Alexandrescu's 2001 HPND-style permission notice; the GitHub mirror has no LICENSE file. Boost.Wave ships a BSL-1.0 copy (boost/wave/util/flex_string.hpp)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 251 stars, 72 forks (GitHub mirror); SourceForge Loki 4.4/5 across 7 reviews; a modified flex_string copy ships in Boost.Wave as boost/wave/util/flex_string.hpp
corrections.caveats: Anecdotal, second-hand number with no methodology, hardware, compiler or standard-library version, from the pre-C++11 era (CUJ articles 2001 and 2005); the page misspells the reporter as 'Harmut Kaizer' (Hartmut Kaiser, Boost.Wave's author) and its first paragraph describes SafeFormat ('Type-Safe Formatting', CUJ July 2005, a printf emulation), apparently a copy-paste error. Boost.Wave adopted flex_string as boost/wave/util/flex_string.hpp under BSL-1.0, and its change log records correctness fixes on top of Alexandrescu's code (#HK030306 'Fixed a string terminating bug in append'), so the 5-10% may predate fixes; modern std::string implementations with SSO (libstdc++ since GCC 5, libc++, MSVC STL) differ from the 2001-era baselines. The project's other components have benchmark code but no published results: test/SmallObj/SmallObjBench.cpp compares Loki::SmallObject with new/delete, malloc and std::allocator (and optionally Boost.Pool) but results must be run locally, and a web snippet reports Loki::AssocVector slower than std::map on insert and lookup in a third-party run. Licence mixed: SourceForge lists MIT and SmallObj.h states MIT, but flex_string.h still carries the older Alexandrescu permission notice (HPND-style, not a verbatim SPDX licence). Last GitHub commit 2013-08-06 ('Improved SmartAssert component.'); SourceForge status Beta, last update 2013-08-06; README targets GCC 3.4-4.1 and MSVC 7.1/8.0.

notes: The 5-10% figure is on the page as stated; it is second-hand with no methodology, so C stays (arguably the weakest C). Metadata checks out (251 stars, no LICENSE in mirror, SourceForge MIT 4.4/5 7 reviews, last update 2013-08-06, abandoned). New fact: Boost.Wave still ships a BSL-1.0 flex_string copy with later correctness fixes; shortcomings to record: anecdotal second-hand claim, pre-SSO-era baseline, abandoned since 2013, mixed licence.
